title: Self-Preservation
hook: The cash-flow sheet made the new program look generous and the next payroll look fragile.
counterintuition: The brave yes can be the reckless one. Self-preservation protects the conditions that let a system keep serving under pressure.
tryThisNow: Before saying yes to one expansion, name the condition it risks. Protect that condition in writing before you accept the new load.
keyTakeaway: Self-preservation protects survival, integrity, and essential conditions before growth or approval can damage the system that must continue.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rebecca's grant receivable looked like good news until the cash-flow sheet showed the money would arrive after payroll. The board wanted to announce the new program. Staff needed the organization to survive the month.

She updated the board minutes with a reserve rule before approving expansion.

Self-preservation protects viability. It is not selfishness by default. A system that cannot preserve its essential conditions loses the ability to help anyone.
breakdown.deepRead:
"We might need that export someday," Steven said, pointing at the old drive. The retention schedule said the opposite. Keeping data too long made the company easier to harm and harder to defend.

The safe frame is direct: self-preservation concerns survival, protection, integrity, defensive structure, and viability under threat. Steven was not resisting useful knowledge. He was protecting the conditions that kept the organization trustworthy. The deletion ticket looked less exciting than a new analytics project, but it defended the system from a threat expansion would ignore. Protection is a form of intelligence.

You cannot serve from a broken container.

Adrien learned it after the first storm in years. The battery pack was dead, the water pouch had leaked, and the weather radio crackled only after fresh batteries were borrowed. The storm kit had seemed paranoid during calm weather. In the postmortem, he saw it differently: maintenance was not fear. It was the defensive structure that kept the household viable when the environment turned.

The limit is rigidity. Self-preservation can become excuse-making when every change is treated as a threat. The model asks what condition must be protected for survival, not how to avoid every discomfort.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 9:18 p.m., Niels stared at the scope clause while a change-order email asked for three extra pages by Friday. The client sounded friendly. The invoice draft said the truth: if he absorbed the work for approval, rent money would come from the next project before it existed.

Self-preservation often feels impolite because it interrupts approval. It asks for a boundary, a reserve, a deletion, a backup, or a protocol before people are done admiring the new opportunity. That interruption can look small-minded from the outside. Inside the system, it may be the thing that keeps payroll, trust, health, or rent intact.

What condition must remain true for this system to keep going?

That question separates protection from panic. Rebecca needed a cash reserve, not a rejection of programs. Steven needed deletion rules, not secrecy. Adrien needed a maintained storm kit, not fear of weather. Niels needed a paid change order, not hostility toward the client. The self-preserving move names the essential condition and defends it before expansion consumes it.

Protection is easiest to misunderstand when the request sounds generous. A new program, a bigger event, a rushed meal, or an extra page can look like service. The self-preserving question asks what the yes will spend: cash, attention, safety, trust, legal exposure, or the capacity of the people holding the system together.

You can feel this in a school club. Aaron holds the teacher key after the sponsor announces a transfer. The room booking looks secure for two weeks, and permission slips are already signed. Without a backup sponsor, the club disappears the day one adult leaves. Adding a bigger event would win attention and make the failure worse. The viable move is boring: update permission slips, name a second sponsor, and keep the club alive before planning the showcase.

Bruno saw the same pattern in a restaurant allergen protocol. A rush order ticket asked for speed, and the prep spoon sat in the wrong container. The allergen matrix was not bureaucracy; it was survival protection for the guest and integrity protection for the kitchen. Saying no to speed in that moment preserved the system that made service possible.

Self-preservation has an ethical shape. It can protect a worthy system, or it can defend a harmful one. The model does not make survival sacred in every case. It tells you to see the protective behavior clearly, then judge whether the system deserves to continue and what conditions must be defended. Protecting viability is responsible only when the viable thing is worth continuing.

When pressure rises, look for the condition expansion is about to consume. Protect that first. Growth that destroys viability is not growth; it is a delayed collapse.

examples.title: Rebecca Writes the Reserve Rule

planSpec.audience: readers who face nonprofit cash reserve rule decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: payroll survival after a late grant
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rebecca protects the condition named on the cash-flow sheet, refuses the expansion hidden in the grant receivable, and updates the board minutes so survival comes before approval. Domain: nonprofit cash reserve rule.

examples.scenario: The cash-flow sheet sticks to Rebecca's wrist while the grant receivable sits in the next column like a promise. Payroll is due before the money arrives. Rebecca faces a choice: announce a new program for applause, or update the board minutes with a reserve rule that protects payroll first.
examples.whatToDo: Write the reserve condition into the board minutes before approving the expansion. Let payroll survival set the boundary.
examples.whyItMatters: The organization cannot serve if it breaks its own viability. Self-preservation protects the condition that keeps the mission alive.

examples.title: Steven Deletes the Export

planSpec.audience: readers who face privacy data-retention review decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: damage from keeping data too long
planSpec.requiredBeat: Steven protects the condition named on the retention schedule, refuses the expansion hidden in the old export drive, and updates the deletion ticket so survival comes before approval. Domain: privacy data-retention review.

examples.scenario: "Keep the old export just in case," the analyst says while Steven reads the retention schedule. The old export drive looks useful until the reveal: it contains data the company no longer has a reason to hold. Steven must decide between possible future convenience and a deletion ticket that protects trust now.
examples.whatToDo: Follow the retention schedule, delete the old export, and record the deletion ticket. Protect integrity before chasing optional analysis.
examples.whyItMatters: Preserving the system sometimes means refusing extra data. Too much retained information becomes a threat.

examples.title: Adrien Rebuilds the Shelf

planSpec.audience: readers who face storm kit maintenance shelf decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: first storm after years of calm
planSpec.requiredBeat: Adrien protects the condition named on the battery pack, refuses the expansion hidden in the water pouch, and updates the weather radio so survival comes before approval. Domain: storm kit maintenance shelf.

examples.scenario: The basement shelf smells like damp cardboard after the storm. Adrien finds a dead battery pack, a leaking water pouch, and a weather radio that works only after borrowing cells from a toy. In the postmortem, he stops treating the kit as clutter and rebuilds the maintenance rule that protects the household.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the battery pack, rotate water, and test the weather radio on a calendar. Maintain the defensive structure before calm returns.
examples.whyItMatters: Protection looks excessive until the threat arrives. The kit preserves viability when ordinary systems fail.

examples.title: Niels Sends the Change Order

planSpec.audience: readers who face freelance contract boundary decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Niels protects the condition named on the scope clause, refuses the expansion hidden in the change-order email, and updates the invoice draft so survival comes before approval. Domain: freelance contract boundary.

examples.scenario: At 9:18 p.m., Niels reads the scope clause while a change-order email asks for three extra pages by Friday. The invoice draft already barely covers rent. Before replying warmly, Niels has to choose between approval and a paid boundary that keeps the project viable.
examples.whatToDo: Send the change order with price and timing before doing the extra work. Protect the rent condition written into the invoice draft.
examples.whyItMatters: A boundary is not fear of clients. It preserves the economic condition that lets the work continue.

examples.title: Aaron Finds the Second Sponsor

planSpec.audience: readers who face school club sponsor backup decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: club disappearing when one teacher leaves
planSpec.requiredBeat: Aaron protects the condition named on the teacher key, refuses the expansion hidden in the room booking, and updates the permission slip so survival comes before approval. Domain: school club sponsor backup.

examples.scenario: You see Aaron holding the teacher key after the club sponsor announces a transfer. The room booking covers two meetings, and the permission slips promise a showcase. Aaron hovers over two paths: plan the bigger event, or find a second sponsor so the club still exists next month.
examples.whatToDo: Name a backup sponsor, update permission slips, and confirm room access before expanding club events.
examples.whyItMatters: The club's survival depends on an adult sponsor. Approval for a showcase means little if the basic condition disappears.

examples.title: Bruno Stops the Ticket

planSpec.audience: readers who face restaurant allergen protocol decisions where self-preservation is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: one mistake risking a severe reaction
planSpec.requiredBeat: Bruno protects the condition named on the allergen matrix, refuses the expansion hidden in the order ticket, and updates the prep spoon so survival comes before approval. Domain: restaurant allergen protocol.

examples.scenario: It took Bruno one near miss to stop treating the allergen matrix as paperwork. "Can we rush table twelve?" the server asks, holding an order ticket while the prep spoon sits in the wrong pan. Bruno must decide now: speed the order, or reset the spoon and protect the protocol.
examples.whatToDo: Pause the ticket, reset the prep spoon, and follow the allergen matrix before serving. Let protection outrank speed.
examples.whyItMatters: The defensive structure preserves guest safety and kitchen integrity. Service that breaks that condition is not service.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit can announce a new program, but the grant cash arrives after payroll and the cash-flow sheet is tight. What does self-preservation protect first?
choices: The cash reserve condition that keeps payroll viable.
The applause from announcing expansion.
The hope that money timing will solve itself.
questions.explanation: Payroll is an essential condition. Expansion that endangers viability weakens the system meant to serve.

questions.prompt: A company wants to keep old customer exports for possible future analysis, but the retention schedule says deletion is due this week. Which move fits the model?
choices: Keep everything because more data always helps.
Delete the export and record the deletion ticket to protect integrity.
Hide the drive so no one has to decide.
questions.explanation: The retention rule preserves trust and reduces threat. Keeping data for optional convenience can damage the system.

questions.prompt: A storm kit has dead batteries, leaking water pouches, and an untested radio after years of calm weather. What is the self-preserving action?
choices: Assume calm years prove the kit is unnecessary.
Buy decorative storage for the shelf.
Restore the battery, water, and radio maintenance rule before the next threat.
questions.explanation: The kit is a defensive structure. Maintenance protects viability before the threat arrives; calm does not remove the need.

questions.prompt: A freelancer receives extra work outside scope by Friday, and saying yes unpaid would threaten rent shown in the invoice draft. Which response preserves the system?
choices: Absorb the work to stay liked.
Send a priced change order before doing the extra work.
Ignore the client without explanation.
questions.explanation: The boundary protects economic viability. Approval is tempting, but rent is the condition that lets the work continue.

questions.prompt: A school club plans a showcase, but its only teacher sponsor is leaving and room access depends on a teacher key. What should come before expansion?
choices: A bigger event poster to keep enthusiasm high.
A backup sponsor and updated permission slips.
A hope that another adult appears later.
questions.explanation: The club's survival condition is adult sponsorship. Planning more activity before protecting that condition risks disappearance.

questions.prompt: A restaurant rush ticket pressures the kitchen to skip an allergen protocol while the prep spoon sits in the wrong container. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: Protocols matter only when the dining room is quiet.
The guest should accept extra risk during a rush.
Speed is threatening the defensive structure that preserves safety.
questions.explanation: The allergen protocol preserves guest safety and kitchen integrity. Speed that breaks it damages the system.

questions.prompt: A team rejects every change by calling it self-preservation, even when no essential condition, protocol, or reserve is threatened. What is wrong?
choices: They are using protection as a cover for rigidity.
They should never protect existing conditions.
They should approve every expansion immediately.
questions.explanation: Self-preservation protects essential viability. If no condition is threatened, the label may be avoiding discomfort rather than preserving survival.

questions.prompt: A small clinic limits new patient intake until it has enough nurses for safe follow-up, and critics call the limit selfish. How should you evaluate the move?
choices: It may be self-preservation if safe follow-up is the condition that keeps care viable.
It is always selfish to limit growth.
It proves the clinic does not care about patients.
questions.explanation: Protecting the condition for safe care can preserve the system's ability to serve. Growth that breaks follow-up is not healthy expansion.

questions.prompt: A volunteer group wants to add a weekend event, but the core scheduling spreadsheet is broken and leaders are already burning out. What response transfers the model?
choices: Add the event to prove commitment.
Criticize volunteers for needing structure.
Repair the scheduling and leadership capacity before adding load.
questions.explanation: Scheduling and leader capacity are viability conditions. Expansion before protection can collapse the group.

reviewCards.front: An opportunity threatens payroll, trust, safety, or capacity. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve self-preservation: protect the condition that keeps the system viable before accepting expansion.

reviewCards.front: A clinic limits growth to protect safe follow-up. Why is self-preservation not automatically selfish?
reviewCards.back: A system that cannot preserve essential conditions loses the ability to serve, protect, or continue.

reviewCards.front: A team rejects change without naming any threatened condition. When does self-preservation become rigidity?
reviewCards.back: When every change is treated as a threat even though no survival condition is actually at risk.

reviewCards.front: A new opportunity would spend cash, trust, or safety. What should be named before saying yes to growth?
reviewCards.back: Name the viability condition growth might consume, such as cash, safety, trust, capacity, or integrity.

reviewCards.front: Why can a boring protocol be protective intelligence?
reviewCards.back: It preserves the defensive structure that keeps the system intact when pressure rises.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to protect essential conditions before expansion or approval consumes them. The skill is naming viability and defending it in writing.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a new opportunity arrives before cash is secure, then I will protect the reserve condition before approving expansion.
If stored information no longer has a valid purpose, then I will delete it before seeking extra value from it.
If extra scope threatens rent or delivery quality, then I will send a change order before doing the work.
If speed pressures a protective protocol, then I will pause the work and restore the defensive condition first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, find one request for expansion or approval. Write the essential condition it could consume, then protect that condition before answering.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, audit one system you rely on for the condition that keeps it viable: reserve, protocol, backup, boundary, or deletion rule.

memorableLines.why: It reframes self-preservation as judgment rather than fear.

memorableLines.text: You cannot serve from a broken container.
memorableLines.why: It makes viability concrete and memorable.

memorableLines.text: Growth that destroys viability is not growth; it is a delayed collapse.
